migrationNotes: Spine: start from one security rule and two colleagues who read it differently, turn it round two ways, and test each against every case to see which keeps its meaning.
Converse first (shown to differ in one case), then contrapositive (checked row by row), then back to the engineer's file.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): converse-and-contrapositive-3, converse-and-contrapositive-hook, converse-and-contrapositive-contrapositive-check.

lesson.title: Converse and contrapositive

lead.text: Take the policy as it stands. “If a file is encrypted, then it needs a key” has the form p → q, with p for “the file is encrypted” and q for “the file needs a key”. The condition comes first and what follows from it comes second.

Turning a rule round can mean several things, and the simplest is to swap the two halves. That gives “If a file needs a key, then it is encrypted”, which is q → p. A rule made by swapping the antecedent and consequent like this is called the converse of the original.

People often treat the converse as if it were the same rule said differently. The first colleague did exactly that. Whether it says the same thing is what the next few screens test, and the test is simple: look for a case in which the two disagree.

diagram.alt: The security policy as p to q, and its converse, with the two halves swapped, as q to p.
diagram.caption: The policy, and the rule made by swapping its halves. The swapped rule is the converse.

lead.text: Take another rule: “If it rains, the match is cancelled.” Swap its two halves and leave everything else alone.

steps.headline: How to tell two rules apart

lead.text: Two rules say the same thing only if they are true together and false together in every possible case. That gives a way to compare them. Write down every case, work out each rule in it, and look for a case where one is true and the other false. A single case like that is enough to show that the rules differ.

Try the case where the file is encrypted and does need a key, so p and q are both true. The original, p → q, is true, because the condition is met and the result follows. The converse, q → p, is true as well, because its condition q is met and its result p follows. Here the two agree, and that proves nothing, since rules can agree in one case and still differ in another.

So agreement in one case settles nothing, while disagreement in one case settles everything. To tell the converse from the original we need a case where they come apart. The next screen tries a file that needs a key without being encrypted.

diagram.alt: A table of the four rows of p and q with columns for p to q and q to p. Only the first row is filled in, where both rules are true and agree.
diagram.caption: To compare two rules, check them in every row. The first row is done and the rule is the same in it.

lead.text: A file needs a key although it isn't encrypted, so p is false and q is true. The original rule, p → q, only speaks about encrypted files. It holds here.

reveal.text: Your answer shows a case where the original holds and the converse fails. The two rules disagree, so the converse is a different claim. The second colleague was right.

lead.text: Swapping alone changed the meaning, so look for a way of turning the rule round that keeps it. The idea is to run the reasoning backwards. If every encrypted file needs a key, then a file with no key can't be encrypted, because had it been encrypted it would have needed one.

Written out, that is “If a file doesn't need a key, then it isn't encrypted”, which is ¬q → ¬p. Two things were done to the original. The halves were swapped, as for the converse, and each half was negated, using the ¬ from the first lesson. A rule built this way is called the contrapositive of the original.

It is worth checking that this one says the same thing, and the check is the one from before: go through the cases and compare. The next screen does the first two cases for you and leaves the other two to you.

diagram.caption: Start from the original at the top. Swapping only gives the converse. Swapping and negating both halves gives the contrapositive.

steps.headline: Compare p → q with ¬q → ¬p in the two cases where p is true.

lead.text: Both rules need to be worked out in each case. Write ¬q and ¬p first, and then read the rule from them.

workedSteps.text: p true, q true. The original has a true consequent, so it is true. In the other rule ¬q is false, so its condition is not met and it is true.
p true, q false. The original has a true condition and a missing result, so it is false. In the other rule ¬q is true and ¬p is false, so it is false too.

lead.text: The worked example covered the two cases where p is true. Do the two where p is false in the same way, then look across all four cases.

steps.headline: What the contrapositive lets you conclude

lead.text: Because the contrapositive says the same thing, it gives a second way to use any rule. “If a file is encrypted, it needs a key” has the contrapositive “If a file doesn't need a key, it isn't encrypted”. A file that opens without a key must be unencrypted, and the engineer can say so with confidence.

The opposite finding gives no such confidence. A file that needs a key tells you nothing certain, because the converse, “If a file needs a key, it is encrypted”, is a different rule that nobody has said holds. The colleague who said the file must be encrypted was reading the converse into the policy. The other colleague had it right.
Of the two ways to turn a rule round, only one keeps its meaning. Swap the halves and negate both, and the meaning stays. Swap them and leave them alone, and the meaning changes.
A courier's rule: “If a parcel is fragile, then it gets a warning label.”

lesson.orientation: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.
lesson.nextAction: Solve a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it to a contradiction.

blocks.text: A company's security policy says: “If a file is encrypted, then it needs a key to open.” That is the whole rule. An engineer finds a file on the shared drive and discovers that it needs a key to open.

One colleague says the file must be encrypted, since the policy ties encryption to keys. Another says the policy allows no such conclusion. They are reading the same sentence, and only one of them can be right.

Both colleagues are turning the rule round, which people do all the time with rules and promises. There are two common ways to do it. This lesson tests each one against every case, and finds which one says the same thing as the original and which one says something new.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the converse and contrapositive of an if-then rule, and know which one says the same thing.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional says the same thing as its contrapositive, ¬q → ¬p. It does not say the same thing as its converse, q → p.

blocks.text: Back on the shared drive, you found that a file needing a key need not be encrypted. You checked all four cases and found none where p → q and ¬q → ¬p disagree. You also wrote the contrapositive of a courier's rule about fragile parcels.

recap.nextHook: You can now turn a rule round without changing what it says. The next lesson takes that care to a puzzle on an island where some people always lie.

questions.prompt: Is q → p true or false when q is true and p is false?
hints: In q → p, q is the antecedent and p is the consequent.
Is this the case with a true antecedent and a false consequent?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The converse has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: False. In q → p the antecedent q holds and the consequent p fails. p → q is true in this same case.

misconceptions.feedback: In q → p, q comes first. Apply the rule from the last lesson with q as the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Across the four cases, how many differ between p → q and ¬q → ¬p?
hints: Compare each case of p → q with the same case of ¬q → ¬p.
Negate both inputs and swap their order for the second expression.
Count disagreements, not true cases.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their truth values match in every case, so none differ.

questions.onCorrect: None. The two have the same truth value in every case, so the contrapositive says the same thing.

misconceptions.feedback: The worked example showed the false case: it is false in both. Count the cases where they disagree.
Check each case against the matching one for ¬q → ¬p. They fail in the same case.
They don't disagree everywhere. Compare them case by case.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q true but its converse q → p false?
hints: The converse is false only when q is true and p is false.
Check that p → q is still true in that case.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true, p → q is true and q → p is false.

choices.label: p false, q true
p true, q true
p true, q false

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true. The original holds, the converse fails, so the two are not the same claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Both are true here. You need a case where they disagree.
Here p → q is already false. You need it true.

questions.prompt: Choose the contrapositive of “If fragile, then labelled”.
hints: Swap the two parts, then negate both.
The consequent “labelled” becomes the negated antecedent.

acceptedIdeas: If not labelled, then not fragile
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap and negate both: if not labelled, then not fragile.

choices.label: If not labelled, then not fragile
If labelled, then fragile
If not fragile, then not labelled

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if not labelled, then not fragile. It says the same as the original.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but doesn't negate them. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. It isn't the contrapositive.

questions.prompt: What is q → p called relative to p → q?
hints: This swaps the original antecedent and consequent.
It does not negate either claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exchanging the two claims gives the converse.

questions.onCorrect: The converse. The parts are swapped and nothing is negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The contrapositive also negates both parts. Here they are only swapped.

questions.prompt: What is ¬q → ¬p called relative to p → q?
hints: This both swaps the order and negates the claims.
Tell it apart from merely swapping p and q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reversing and negating both claims gives the contrapositive.

questions.onCorrect: The contrapositive. The parts are swapped and both are negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The converse only swaps the parts. Here both are negated as well.

hints: The rule says what encrypted files need. Does it say only encrypted files need one?
Could a file need a key for some other reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily. Other files may need a key too.

questions.onCorrect: Not necessarily. “If encrypted, then key” doesn't say that a key means encrypted. Turning a rule round changes it.

choices.label: Yes, it must be.
Not necessarily.
No, it can't be.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what encrypted files need. It doesn't say that only encrypted files need one.
The rule doesn't rule encryption out. It just doesn't settle it.

questions.prompt: Why is ¬q → ¬p false in this row?
hints: Work out ¬q and ¬p for this row first.
What makes any conditional false?

acceptedIdeas: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ¬q is true and ¬p is false, which is the one case that breaks a conditional.

questions.onCorrect: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: the same broken-promise pattern, reached by negating and swapping.

choices.label: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
Swapping the parts never changes a conditional.
A negated claim is always false.

misconceptions.feedback: Swapping alone does change a conditional. That is why the converse differs. Look at ¬q and ¬p.
¬ flips a value. It doesn't fix it.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If it's a square, it has four sides.” A shape does not have four sides. What follows?
hints: Write the contrapositive of the rule first.
The contrapositive starts from “not four sides”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive says: if it doesn't have four sides, it isn't a square.

questions.onCorrect: Not a square. The contrapositive says the same as the rule: no four sides, so not a square.

choices.label: It is not a square.
It is a square.
Nothing follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs against the rule: squares have four sides.
The rule's contrapositive starts from exactly this fact.

questions.prompt: What is the converse of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: The converse swaps the two parts and negates nothing.

acceptedIdeas: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap the parts: if the match is cancelled, it rains.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate nothing: if the match is cancelled, it rains.

choices.label: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.
If it rains, the match is played.

misconceptions.feedback: That negates both parts but keeps the order. The converse only swaps.
That keeps the order and negates one part. The converse only swaps the parts.

questions.prompt: What is the contrapositive of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: Swap the parts, then negate both.

acceptedIdeas: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap and negate both parts: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

choices.label: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but negates neither. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. The contrapositive also swaps them.
